newsitem.title: USA: Rubin says U.S. benefits from trade ties with China.
newsitem.headline: Rubin says U.S. benefits from trade ties with China.

text.p: U.S. economic and security interests are better served by maintaining normal trade relations with China than by revoking trade privileges as some lawmakers would like, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Thursday.

In a speech to the U.S.-China Business Council, Rubin said taking away Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status from China would hurt U.S. consumers, undermine U.S. interests in the region and harm efforts to promote stability in Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.

"Severing trade ties with China will not isolate China. It will isolate the United States," Rubin said, adding that it would hurt ability to participate in the fastest growing economic region in the world.
"Revoking normal trade relations with China would also harm Hong Kong in the name of supporting it," Rubin said.

He noted that a coalition of Hong Kong human rights leaders, the current government in Hong Kong and others have warned that cutting trade ties with China would be "exactly the wrong step if our objective is to preserve an autonomous and free Hong Kong."

Earlier this week, Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, introduced a resolution to deny China MFN trade status. A growing trade deficit with China as well as concerns about human rights and Hong Kong's future under Chinese rule has helped fuel U.S. lawmakers' sentiment against China.
House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri also opposes renewal of China's MFN status.

Rubin said he realised that many Americans feel they are unable to compete with low wage workers in China. But he said that means lower cost goods for American consumers and noted that China in turn buys airplanes and other high-end goods from the United States.

"As a highly productive and competitive economy, the United States can -- and does -- trade with low wage countries, including China, and the benefits of increasing trade with these countries vastly outweigh the disadvantages," he said.

Rubin said he believed the vote in the House of Representatives this year would be closer than last year, but that President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's trade status for another year would be upheld.
"My best guess in the final analysis is the House will not vote to revoke MFN," Rubin told reporters after his speech.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told reporters after speaking to a different group that members of Congress understood the dangers of being the only nation in the world to sever economic ties with China.
"There is in the House a growing appreciation that to cut off MFN is to isolate ourselves with China," Barshefsky said. "That really is the only effect of cutting off MFN."
The House is expected to vote first on the China MFN issue. Last year the Senate never voted on China MFN status after it was upheld in the House by a wide margin.
